drills.q: Adding more worker threads to a CPU-bound pipeline doesn't improve throughput, or makes it slightly worse. Diagnose.
drills.a: ThreadPoolExecutor was used for genuinely CPU-bound work on a standard GIL-enabled build -- the GIL still serializes bytecode execution, and extra threads only add scheduling/contention overhead with no parallelism benefit. Fix: switch to ProcessPoolExecutor, or a verified-compatible free-threaded build.

drills.q: A multiprocessing pipeline with many small, frequent task submissions runs slower than expected. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Pickling/unpickling overhead per task dominates when payloads are small and numerous, since serialization cost is paid on every exchange regardless of how little computation each task does. Fix: batch multiple units of work into larger per-task submissions to amortize the fixed serialization cost over more actual computation.

drills.q: A team migrates to the free-threaded Python build and sees intermittent crashes that never occurred on the standard GIL build. What's the likely cause and how do you investigate?
drills.a: A C extension dependency likely relied implicitly on the GIL's protection for its own internal state and hasn't been verified thread-safe without it. Investigate by identifying C-extension-backed dependencies in the crashing code's hot path, checking their free-threading compatibility status, and isolating/removing that dependency to confirm it's the source before assuming an application-code bug.

drills.q: How would you catch a 'wrong executor for the workload' (ThreadPoolExecutor used for CPU-bound work) mistake in code review or testing, given that it produces no error?
drills.a: A purely functional/correctness test suite passes either way since the bug is a performance characteristic, not a correctness one. Catch it with a performance regression test or benchmark comparing expected scaling (wall-clock time should drop roughly proportionally with worker count for genuinely parallel work) against actual measured scaling.

drills.q: Design a data pipeline (file read -> CPU-bound parse/transform -> DB write) for a standard GIL-enabled build, then explain what changes if all dependencies are confirmed free-threading-compatible.
drills.a: On GIL-enabled: ProcessPoolExecutor for the CPU-bound parse/transform stage (genuine parallelism), threading or asyncio for the I/O-bound read/write stages, batching data crossing into the process pool to amortize pickling cost. On a fully-compatible free-threaded build: the CPU-bound stage could use ThreadPoolExecutor instead, sharing memory directly and avoiding the pickling/serialization cost multiprocessing requires.

drills.q: A dependency in your CPU-bound pipeline stage is confirmed NOT free-threading-safe, but you want some benefit today. What's a reasonable middle-ground architecture?
drills.a: Keep the CPU-bound stage on ProcessPoolExecutor (works regardless of free-threading support) while using asyncio/threading for I/O-bound stages, treating migration of the CPU-bound stage to a free-threaded ThreadPoolExecutor as a separate future step gated on confirming that specific dependency's compatibility -- avoiding taking on free-threading's risk where multiprocessing already adequately parallelizes.

drills.q: A colleague argues 'once free-threaded Python is the default, we'll never need multiprocessing again.' What's wrong with this claim?
drills.a: Free-threading solves CPU parallelism within a single process on a single machine only. It provides no fault isolation (a crash/corruption in one thread can take down the whole process, unlike separate processes) and no multi-machine scaling -- both remain reasons multiprocessing (or distributed processes) stays relevant even after broad free-threading adoption.

drills.q: Does multiprocessing.shared_memory make concurrent writes from multiple worker processes automatically safe?
drills.a: No -- shared_memory only provides the underlying memory-sharing mechanism to avoid redundant per-worker copies of large read-heavy data. It provides no synchronization; concurrent writes from multiple processes still need an explicit Lock, the same category of problem (concurrent shared-state mutation) that originally motivated the GIL.
